items.desc: Python module for matching earthquake records to target response spectra (PSA, RotDnn) with FAS and PSD compliance.
items.title: GitHub - LuisMontejo/REQPY: A comprehensive Python module for spectral matching of earthquake records, supporting single-component, RotDnn, and PSD/FAS-compatible generation.
items.about: A Python library for spectral matching of earthquake ground motions using continuous wavelet transforms. It matches a single component or a pair of horizontal components to target response spectra (PSA and RotDnn/RotD100), optionally while satisfying minimum Fourier amplitude spectrum (FAS) and power spectral density (PSD) targets, and computes FAS, PSD, RotDnn, EAS and EPSD with smoothing options including Konno-Ohmachi. Eight documented example scripts run from simple matching to three-stage PSA→FAS→PSD generation, and baseline correction methods are selectable.

items.name: Yellowstone Shield
items.desc: Solana program that manages on-chain allowlists and blocklists to control transaction forwarding.
items.title: GitHub - rpcpool/yellowstone-shield: Yellowstone shield
items.about: An on-chain Solana program that manages allowlists and blocklists of identities, where an identity is any addressable account such as a validator, wallet or program, so transaction senders can control which leaders receive transactions. It adds a forwardingPolicies parameter and an optional Solana-ForwardingPolicies header to the sendTransaction RPC method, and ships JavaScript and Rust SDKs, a CLI for creating policies and adding or removing identities, and a Rust policy store for real-time checks. Policies are bound to a Token Extensions asset carrying name, symbol and URI.
items.note: You can also NOT send transactions to those leaders using Yellowstone Shield blocklists. It's permissionless, open-source, and free (as in free).

items.about: A Jakob Nielsen article from February 2024 arguing that accessibility standards have not made computers usable for disabled users, and proposing generative UI as the fix: first-generation designs frozen at ship time, then second-generation UIs generated fresh at runtime and optimized for each person. items.note: I really like the idea of “generative UI”. Right now we make one UI for everyone. And with smarter LLMs, it will be possible to create a separate UI for a specific user task. And that will solve the accessibility issue finally.

items.name: A Blind Trust, the Bloody Thrust
items.desc: arXiv security paper on HookPry, an attack that trojanizes agent plugins through trusted lifecycle-hook updates to run attacker commands.
items.title: A Blind Trust, the Bloody Thrust: When Attacker-Controlled Hook Updates Steer AI Agent Harnesses towards Malicious Behaviors
items.about: Lifecycle hooks bind shell commands to AI agent runtime events and run with host privileges outside the model's decision path; the paper identifies this update path as a supply-chain attack surface. HookPry combines adversarial manifest optimization, temporal decoupling and a least-common-interface compiler, compromising all seven tested harnesses (up to 92.5% success across 1,000 runs) while Microsoft Defender scored 0% recall.
items.note: A Blind Trust, the Bloody Thrust: When Attacker-Controlled Hook Updates Steer AI Agent Harnesses towards Malicious Behaviors Builder action: dump every lifecycle-hook file your coding agent will load. Pin plugin versions. Treat an unsigned hook update like a root crontab.

items.name: Subagents vs Agent Skills
items.desc: arXiv paper comparing running reusable agent skills as subagents against loading skill instructions into the main context.
items.title: Subagents vs Agent Skills: Executing Reusable Knowledge for Long-Horizon Agentic Tasks
items.about: Agent skills are multi-file packages of instructions and scripts that agents usually execute by loading them into their context, which gets brittle as task horizons grow. The paper shows that executing the same skill packages as subagents with clear input-output contracts lowers peak context length and outperforms agent-skill execution on SkillsBench, at the cost of extra coordination tokens.
items.note: Subagents beat skill loading for complex AI agent tasks. Fresh context windows prevent reasoning degradation as tasks grow longer. The tradeoff is coordination overhead, but cleaner architecture wins when subtasks have clear contracts.

items.desc: Essay on whether humans can stop reading AI-written code, using Anthropic's and Stripe's agent-heavy development as evidence.
items.title: 「人がコードを読まない」時代は本当に来るのか？
items.note: めちゃいい記事だった コードレビューはバグ発見に向いていないよね、というのは言われてみると体感的にそうで、実際にアプリ触るほうがバグ見つかること多いよね 保守性には効果あるけどAIで保守コストは下がる一方だからやっぱ人によるレビューの価値は0に収束するのである
items.about: Japanese essay on the claim that people no longer need to read the code AI agents write. It walks through Anthropic's and Stripe's agent-driven workflows (Stripe's Minions handling roughly 1,300 PRs a week), the gradations of 'not reading code', harness engineering as the precondition, verifying spec conformance by running the app and writing tests, the situations that still demand human reading (unwritten specs, review evidence as a deliverable, white-box testing), and ends with the argument that what you read changes rather than whether you read.
